\title{Measured Edge-Inference Energy Versus Quality-Driven Carbon, Material, and Workload Effects of AI Defect Inspection in Manufacturing}

\author{Utkarsh~Sengar%
\thanks{U.~Sengar is with the Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Dharwad, Karnataka 580011, India (e-mail: cs23bt026@iitdh.ac.in).}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Edge AI inspection is often assumed to be green because it prevents scrap; critics counter that always-on inference consumes electricity. We quantify both sides with a conservation-checked accounting model that compares four edge-AI alert policies with no inspection and manual end-of-line inspection. Its key inputs are measured or sourced: the electricity of a real PatchCore pipeline at a 30~FPS line rate (\FullTotalPower~W on an NVIDIA \GpuName{}), the detector's recall and false-positive rate on \DetCategories{} MVTec~AD categories, the alert rates of the policies from our companion alarm-management study, and material, freight and hardware factors from public life-cycle sources. In three reference scenarios the edge cell accounts for at most \EdgeOfBenefitMax\% of the full policy's benefit over manual inspection, which is positive in at least \PrecMcProb\% of \MonteCarloDraws{} Monte Carlo draws; for a lightweight polymer part the benefit is small and vanishes on grids above \PrecGammaStar~kgCO$_2$e/kWh. Because carbon is exactly affine in the number of defects, the analysis reduces to a general rule: inspect when defect prevalence times the carbon saved per defect exceeds the edge cell's carbon per part. Across \PopSize{} sampled products the full policy beats no inspection in \PopWinNZero\% and manual inspection in \PopWinLZero\% of cases. Single-frame alerting would need tens to hundreds of reviewers, so alert design matters more than compute. And carbon-optimal detection thresholds are far more permissive than conventional alarm budgets: for high-value parts they cut up to \HiValOptSavingCapMax~\kgce{} per 1{,}000 parts without additional reviewers.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Sustainable manufacturing, edge AI, industrial anomaly detection, energy measurement, carbon accounting, alarm management, uncertainty analysis.
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
\IEEEPARstart{A}{utomated} optical inspection with unsupervised anomaly detectors such as PatchCore and PaDiM~\cite{roth2022patchcore,defard2021padim} is now accurate enough on public benchmarks~\cite{bergmann2021mvtec} for deployment on edge computers beside production lines. Two opposing sustainability narratives surround these deployments. One holds that inspection is intrinsically ``green'' because intercepted defects are reworked instead of scrapped. The other, prompted by the rapid growth of machine-learning energy use~\cite{strubell2020energy,desislavov2023trends}, asks whether always-on inference erodes those gains. Neither claim is usually quantified for an actual production line, and published estimates rarely separate measured quantities from assumptions. A third factor is usually left out: a detector that alerts on every frame can bury the operators who must act on its alerts.

We ask three questions for a functional unit of 1{,}000 inspected parts:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{Magnitude.} How large is the measured electricity and embodied-hardware footprint of an edge inference cell relative to the material, rework, workload and field-escape effects that inspection changes?
\item \emph{Counterfactual.} Against which baseline---no inspection or manual end-of-line inspection---and under which defect prevalence, compute budget and grid intensity does edge AI stop being carbon-beneficial?
\item \emph{Policy.} With identical compute, how do measured alert policies change operator workload and carbon, and how much recall may temporal filtering lose before it stops paying off?
\end{enumerate}

This paper makes four contributions:
\begin{itemize}
\item An open, conservation-checked accounting model with explicit counterfactual baselines (no inspection, manual inspection) and four AI alert policies, driven by one validated parameter ledger (Tables~\ref{tab:parameters} and~\ref{tab:policies}) whose provenance classes are reported (\RegistryMeasuredCount{} measured, \RegistryPaperACount{} imported from our alert-policy study, \RegistryLiteratureCount{} literature, \RegistryOfficialCount{} official dataset, \RegistryAssumptionCount{} scenario assumptions).
\item Measured inputs instead of assumed ones: line-rate power of a real PatchCore pipeline, with a protocol that respects the refresh limits of on-board GPU sensors~\cite{yang2024accurate}, and per-part recall and false-positive rates of the same detector on \DetCategories{} MVTec~AD categories.
\item A closed-form decision rule, $\pi\beta>k$, that generalises the three reference scenarios, validated on a population of \PopSize{} sampled products and complemented by break-even frontiers, partial-rank-correlation sensitivity and a weight-robust multi-criteria index.
\item Two links between alarm management and sustainability: alert policy dominates operator load, temporal filtering pays off only within a quantified recall-loss margin, and carbon-optimal detection thresholds differ sharply from conventional alarm budgets.
\end{itemize}

\section{Related Work}
\emph{Industrial anomaly detection.} MVTec~AD~\cite{bergmann2021mvtec} established the standard benchmark; PatchCore~\cite{roth2022patchcore} and PaDiM~\cite{defard2021padim} use pretrained CNN patch features with nearest-neighbour or Gaussian scoring. Our earlier work benchmarks cost-calibrated thresholding~\cite{sengar2026flagship1}. A companion study~\cite{sengar2026paperA} turns PatchCore scores into operator alerts through exponential smoothing, $k$-of-$N$ persistence, machine-state gating, divergence triage and an incident latch, and measures eight policy variants on simulated inspection workloads. On good parts, single-frame thresholding raised \PaperAFaRaw{} false alerts per hour and the full policy \PaperAFaFull{}; a sustained defect produced \PaperAPerDefectRaw{} alerts under thresholding and \PaperAPerDefectFull{} under the full policy, at a mean delay of \PaperADelay{} frames. We import those per-policy measurements, with their confidence intervals, and the study's reviewer service rate.

\emph{Energy of machine learning.} Energy accounting for ML has concentrated on training and data-centre inference~\cite{strubell2020energy,henderson2020towards,desislavov2023trends}. On-board NVIDIA sensors are convenient, but on some architectures they sample only part of the runtime, and they refresh at limited rates~\cite{yang2024accurate}. Long, steady-state measurement windows mitigate both problems.

\emph{Manufacturing material and energy efficiency.} Material production dominates the energy of many products~\cite{gutowski2013energy}, and material efficiency---including yield improvement and scrap avoidance---is a recognised mitigation lever~\cite{allwood2011material,ashby2012materials}. ISO~14040/14044 standardise life-cycle assessment practice~\cite{finkbeiner2006new}. Human visual inspection typically misses 20--30\% of defects~\cite{see2012visual}; this range bounds our manual baseline. We know of no work that places measured edge-inference energy and measured alert loads on the same functional unit as these quality-driven flows.

\section{Accounting Model}
\subsection{Functional Unit, Regimes and Boundary}
The functional unit (FU) is $N=1{,}000$ consecutively produced parts. A line with throughput $\Theta$ [parts/h] needs $T_{FU}=N/\Theta$ hours to produce one FU. The gate-to-gate boundary (Fig.~\ref{fig:boundary}) covers inspection electricity, operator-review or manual-inspection workstations, rework electricity, the embodied carbon of unrecovered scrap, the processing burden of recovered scrap, the amortised embodied carbon of the edge hardware, and the consequences of field escapes. Facility base loads, logistics of good parts and labour-related emissions are identical across regimes, so we exclude them. Electricity carries location-based grid factors.

Six regimes enter the comparison. \emph{N0}: no inspection. \emph{L0}: 100\% manual end-of-line visual inspection with recall $r_{L0}$, discovery delay $d_{L0}$ and $t_{L0}$ seconds per part. \emph{B0--B3}: a continuously running edge AI cell under one of the four alert policies measured in~\cite{sengar2026paperA}: single-frame thresholding (B0), exponential smoothing (B1), smoothing with $k$-of-$N$ persistence (B2), and the full policy, which adds an incident latch, machine-state gating and divergence triage (B3). The cell diverts flagged parts automatically and an operator reviews every alert afterwards, so review queues do not delay interception.

\subsection{Defect Routing and Reworkability}
With prevalence $\pi$ the FU contains $D=N\pi$ defects in classes A (reworkable), B (scrap-prone) and C (escape-sensitive) with shares $f_A,f_B,f_C$. A regime with recall $r$ and interception delay $d$ [s] yields
\begin{align}
N_{rw} &= f_A\, r D\, q_{rw}(d), \quad q_{rw}(d) = q_0\, e^{-d/\tau_{rw}}, \label{eq:rw}\\
N_{sc} &= rD - N_{rw}, \qquad N_{esc} = (1-r)D, \label{eq:sc}
\end{align}
where $q_0$ is the zero-delay reworkability and $\tau_{rw}$ the time constant with which a defective part advances into irreversible downstream operations. By construction $N_{rw}+N_{sc}+N_{esc}=D$, and the implementation checks this identity numerically at every evaluation. For L0, $r=r_{L0}$ and $d=d_{L0}$. For an AI policy $t$, $d=d_t/f_{cam}$ with the measured mean delay $d_t$ in frames, and $r=r_{AI}-\delta_r$, where $r_{AI}$ is the detector's recall and $\delta_r$ is a recall loss charged only to the persistence policies B2 and B3. The companion study observed no such loss---all four policies detected every sustained defect---so $\delta_r$ is centred on zero and studied as a break-even parameter.

\subsection{Material, Workload and Energy}
Scrap mass is $M_{gr}=N_{sc}m$ for part mass $m$, of which $M_{rec}=\eta M_{gr}$ is recovered and $M_{loss}=(1-\eta)M_{gr}$ lost. We adopt the operator-load model of~\cite{sengar2026paperA}: every alert reaches the review queue. For policy $t$ the false-alert rate is $\lambda_{FA}=\lambda_t+g\,b_t$, where $\lambda_t$ [1/h] is the measured rate on good parts, $b_t$ the measured alerts per glare burst and $g$ [1/h] the rate of glare bursts. Each detected defect raises $a_t$ alerts. The operator therefore reviews $n_{ev}=\lambda_{FA}T_{FU}+a_t\,rD$ alerts per FU, giving
\begin{equation}
H = \frac{n_{ev}\, t_{review}}{3600}\ \text{[h/FU]}, \qquad \rho = \frac{n_{ev}\, t_{review}}{3600\, T_{FU}},
\end{equation}
where $t_{review}$ [s] is the time to review one alert and $\rho$ is the utilisation of a single operator; for L0, $H=N t_{L0}/3600$ and $\rho=\Theta t_{L0}/3600$; for N0, $H=0$. Electricity per FU [kWh] is
\begin{align}
E_{edge} &= (P_{idle}+P_{active}+P_{host})\,T_{FU}/1000, \\
E_{rev} &= H\,P_{station}/1000, \qquad E_{rw} = N_{rw}\,e_{rw},
\end{align}
with $E_{edge}=0$ for N0 and L0. $P_{idle}$ and $P_{active}$ are the measured GPU powers at the camera rate (Section~\ref{sec:measure}); $P_{host}$ covers host computer, camera and lighting, which NVML cannot observe.

\subsection{Carbon}
Carbon per FU is the sum of seven non-negative components,
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
C ={}& M_{loss}EF_{mat} + M_{rec}EF_{rec} + \gamma\,(E_{rw}+E_{rev}+E_{edge}) \\
& + C_{hw}T_{FU}/L_{hw} + N_{esc}\,(m\,EF_{mat}+c_{ret}) \\
& + \kappa f_C N_{esc}\, m\,EF_{mat},
\end{split}
\end{equation}
where $EF_{mat}$ is the cradle-to-gate material factor, $EF_{rec}$ the processing burden of recovered scrap, $\gamma$ the grid intensity, $C_{hw}$ and $L_{hw}$ the embodied carbon and service life of the edge computer (the hardware term, like $E_{edge}$, is zero for N0 and L0), and each escaped part is replaced (its material is lost) and shipped back, with return and replacement road freight $c_{ret}=2\,(m/1000)\,d_{ret}\,EF_{fr}$ at GLEC intensities $EF_{fr}$ [kgCO$_2$e/t-km]~\cite{glec2023}; class-C escapes add collateral damage $\kappa\, m\,EF_{mat}$. Escape consequences scale with the part; they are not a fixed penalty. For any regime $p$ and baseline $b$, savings are $\Delta X = X_b - X_p$ for $X\in\{M_{loss},E,C,H\}$. The carbon saving $\Delta C$ decomposes exactly into the seven component differences, which we verify to machine precision.

\subsection{A General Decision Rule}
Every term of $C$ is either linear in the defect count $D$ (routing, material, rework, escapes, defect alerts) or independent of it (edge electricity, hardware, false-alert review, manual inspection). For any policy $p$ and baseline $b$, therefore,
\begin{equation}
\Delta C(\pi) = N\pi\,\beta - F, \qquad \pi^\star = \frac{F}{N\beta},
\label{eq:rule}
\end{equation}
where $\beta$ is the net carbon saved per defect and $F$ the fixed carbon per functional unit. For an AI policy against no inspection, $F/N = k$ is the edge cell's carbon per part,
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
k = \frac{1}{\Theta}\Big[&\frac{\gamma(P_{idle}+P_{active}+P_{host})}{1000} + \frac{C_{hw}}{L_{hw}} \\
&+ \frac{\gamma\,\lambda_{FA}\,t_{review}P_{station}}{3.6\times10^{6}}\Big],
\end{split}
\end{equation}
and $\beta = r\,[\,m\,EF_{mat}(1+\kappa f_C)+c_{ret}-h\,]$, where $h$ is the carbon of handling an intercepted defect (scrap and recycling, rework electricity, alert review). Edge AI is carbon-beneficial exactly when $\pi\beta>k$: a defect rate times a per-defect saving must exceed a per-part cost that falls with line throughput. The implementation obtains $\beta$ and $F$ from two model evaluations, so~(\ref{eq:rule}) holds for every parameter set.

\subsection{Sustainability Quality Index}
For the four dimensions, all non-negative by construction, the bounded sub-indicators are $S_X=(X_b-X_p)/\max(X_b,X_p)\in[-1,1]$ ($S_X=0$ when $X_b=X_p=0$), and $\mathrm{SQI}=\sum_X w_X S_X$ with four stakeholder weight profiles (balanced, material-, carbon- and human-centred). Any scalarisation embeds value judgements, so we also report the share of the whole weight simplex (uniform Dirichlet samples) for which $\mathrm{SQI}>0$.

\subsection{Parameters and Uncertainty}
Tables~\ref{tab:parameters} and~\ref{tab:policies} list all \RegistryEntries{} parameter entries with central value, bounds, unit, provenance class and source; both tables are generated from the ledger file and cannot drift from the code. The alert-policy entries are the means and 95\% bootstrap intervals reported in~\cite{sengar2026paperA}, imported from one pinned revision of its artifact; the review time is centred on its service rate of \PaperAMu{} reviews/h and the glare rate on its assumed \PaperAGlareRate{} bursts/h. Grid intensity is centred on the EU-27 2023 value (0.242~kg/kWh~\cite{ember2024}), with the Indian FY2022--23 weighted average (0.716~kg/kWh~\cite{cea2024}) as upper bound. Material factors come from the ICE inventory~\cite{ice2011} and the International Aluminium Institute~\cite{iai2023}, the battery-module factor from~\cite{ivl2019}, the embodied carbon and lifetime of the edge computer from a manufacturer footprint~\cite{dell2021optiplex}, and freight intensities from the GLEC Framework~\cite{glec2023} with return distances from Eurostat road-freight statistics~\cite{eurostat2026road}. Defect prevalence is anchored in measured scrap rates: visual moulding defects per resin at a production injection-moulding plant (2.5--9.3\%)~\cite{nguyen2004injection} for scenario~A, and the global Li-ion manufacturing scrap rate (7.67\% in 2023, projected 4.34\% by 2030)~\cite{yu2024scrap} for scenario~C; a public semiconductor line reports 104 failures in 1{,}567 units (6.6\%)~\cite{secom2008}. Recycling burdens come from a post-industrial plastics recycling inventory~\cite{ruggeri2025postindustrial}, the electricity use of EU mechanical recycling plants~\cite{jrc2023plastics}, and industrial Li-ion recycling~\cite{machala2025recycling}. Reworkability, rework energy, line throughput and manual-inspection timing remain scenario assumptions. We propagate uncertainty with \MonteCarloDraws{} independent triangular draws on the ledger bounds (seed 42) and rank global sensitivity with partial rank correlation coefficients (PRCC)~\cite{marino2008methodology}. Brent's method solves each break-even frontier ($\Delta C=0$) on a physically bounded interval; where $\Delta C$ does not change sign, we report ``none'' together with that sign.

\section{Edge Inference Power Measurement}
\label{sec:measure}
\subsection{Workload and Protocol}
The workload is the PatchCore detector of~\cite{sengar2026paperA}: an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18, layer-2 and layer-3 features pooled to $28\times28\times384$ patch descriptors, exact 1-nearest-neighbour search against a memory bank, and the Gaussian-smoothed maximum as image score, for $224\times224$ RGB frames at batch size~1 in FP32 (PyTorch \TorchVersion, CUDA \CudaRuntime, driver \GpuDriver, WSL2). The bank is a greedy coreset of $\PaperABank$ real patch features from \BenchFitImages{} good \BenchCategory{} training images, the size used in~\cite{sengar2026paperA}, and the stream cycles through \BenchFrames{} real \BenchCategory{} test frames, good and defective. We measured four cumulative stages: the model alone; plus score thresholding; plus a temporal policy (exponential smoothing, $k$-of-$N$ persistence and cooldown); and the full pipeline with SQLite write-ahead-log event persistence and JSON serialisation. Each stage ran paced at the line rate of \BenchFps~FPS for \BenchWindow~s windows, in \BenchRepeats{} repeats with a seeded random stage order, and a 15~s idle window preceded every repeat. We sampled GPU power with NVML at 20~Hz and integrated it over each window; every stage window contains at least \StageReadingsMin{} distinct sensor readings (idle windows at least \IdleReadingsMin). We also logged the NVML cumulative energy counter but do not use it: under WSL2 it reported \CounterIdleMinW--\CounterIdleMaxW~W at idle, inconsistent with the power sensor. We report the median across repeats, with the minimum and maximum as bounds. The GPU also drives the host desktop; windows disturbed by desktop activity remain in the bounds and in the raw data.

\subsection{Results}
Fig.~\ref{fig:energy} shows that at \BenchFps~FPS the stages are indistinguishable: median total power ranges over \StageSpreadW~W, against an idle level of \IdlePower~W. The full pipeline draws \FullTotalPower~W in total and \FullActivePower~W above idle (bounds \FullActivePowerMin--\FullActivePowerMax~W), or \FullFrameEnergy~J per frame above idle (\FullFrameEnergyMin--\FullFrameEnergyMax~J). Thresholding, the temporal policy and event logging add no measurable GPU energy, consistent with the sub-millisecond policy step reported in~\cite{sengar2026paperA}. Unpaced, the model alone reaches \InferMaxFps~FPS and the full pipeline \FullMaxFps~FPS. Median per-frame latency at \BenchFps~FPS is \FullLatencyMs~ms, comparable to the \PaperAVisionLatency~ms vision stage reported in~\cite{sengar2026paperA}, whose \PaperALatency~ms end-to-end cycle additionally includes CPU-side PNG decoding, an optical check and sensor processing that our GPU measurement does not cover. With the $P_{host}$ allowance, one edge cell draws a few tens of watts. That corresponds to $E_{edge}$ between \PrecEdgeKWh{} and \HiValEdgeKWh~kWh per FU, depending on how long the line takes to produce one FU.

\section{Detector Operating Points}
\label{sec:detector}
The same detector, fitted per category, provides the recall the accounting needs. For each of \DetCategories{} MVTec~AD categories~\cite{bergmann2021mvtec} and \DetSeeds{} random splits, 60\% of the good training images build the memory bank (10\% coreset, \DetBankMin--\DetBankMax{} patches), 20\% calibrate thresholds, and the remaining 20\% join the good test images as nominal evaluation data (at least \DetGoodEvalMin{} images per category); defective test images give per-part recall. Table~\ref{tab:detector} and Fig.~\ref{fig:detector} (left) report the results. AUROC lies between \DetAurocMin{} and \DetAurocMax, in line with published PatchCore results~\cite{roth2022patchcore}. At the 99th percentile of the calibration scores (q99), recall ranges from \DetRecallMin{} (\DetWorstCategory) to \DetRecallMax{} at false-positive rates of \DetFprMin--\DetFprMax\%. The ledger's detector recall $r_{AI}$ is the median over categories, \DetRecallMedian, with the category range as bounds. Recall is measured per image, which is conservative for stations that see a part in several frames, and nominal-image counts limit the resolution of false-positive rates to about one percent.

\section{Results}
\subsection{Regime Comparison}
Table~\ref{tab:regimes} and Fig.~\ref{fig:regimes} summarise the six regimes at central parameter values. Relative to manual inspection, the full policy B3 reduces carbon by \PrecRelCarbonReduction\%, \MetalRelCarbonReduction\% and \HiValRelCarbonReduction\% in scenarios A, B and C ($\Delta C=\PrecDeltaCvsLZero$, \MetalDeltaCvsLZero{} and \HiValDeltaCvsLZero~\kgce{} per FU) and reduces unrecovered material ($\Delta M=\PrecDeltaMvsLZero$, \MetalDeltaMvsLZero{} and \HiValDeltaMvsLZero~kg). It uses \emph{more} electricity ($\Delta E=\PrecDeltaEvsLZero$, $\MetalDeltaEvsLZero$ and $\HiValDeltaEvsLZero$~kWh), almost all of it rework electricity: prompt interception keeps defects reworkable that manual end-of-line inspection finds too late. It also needs more operator time than manual inspection ($\Delta H=\PrecDeltaHvsLZero$, $\MetalDeltaHvsLZero$ and $\HiValDeltaHvsLZero$~h), because every alert, including those caused by glare, takes a full review. Without the incident latch the picture changes completely: single-frame thresholding (B0) produces $\rho=\PrecRhoBZero$, \MetalRhoBZero{} and \HiValRhoBZero{}, i.e.\ it would need \PrecReviewersBZero, \MetalReviewersBZero{} and \HiValReviewersBZero{} reviewers. In scenario~A the resulting workstation electricity makes B0 emit more than manual inspection (\PrecCarbonBZero{} vs \PrecCarbonLZero~\kgce{}). B3 stays below one reviewer in scenarios B and C but needs \PrecReviewersBThree{} in scenario~A ($\rho=\PrecRhoBThree$), whose defect rate exceeds the roughly \PaperALoadCross{} defect episodes per hour that~\cite{sengar2026paperA} found one reviewer can absorb.

\subsection{What Drives the Carbon Benefit}
The waterfall in Fig.~\ref{fig:waterfall} decomposes $\Delta C$ (B3 vs L0). Avoided field escapes contribute \PrecEscapeShare\%, \MetalEscapeShare\% and \HiValEscapeShare\%, followed by avoided unrecovered material; rework electricity is the largest negative term. Edge electricity and amortised edge hardware together amount to \PrecEdgeCarbon, \MetalEdgeCarbon{} and \HiValEdgeCarbon~\kgce{} per FU---\PrecEdgeOfBenefit\%, \MetalEdgeOfBenefit\% and \HiValEdgeOfBenefit\% of the benefit and at most \EdgeShareMax\% of B3's total footprint. The compute side is roughly two to three orders of magnitude smaller than the benefit. Recall, and what an escaped defect costs, decide the outcome.

\subsection{Break-Even Frontiers}
Table~\ref{tab:uncertainty} and Fig.~\ref{fig:breakeven} report where $\Delta C=0$. Against no inspection, the edge cell pays back its electricity, hardware and review carbon once prevalence exceeds \PrecPiStarNZero, \MetalPiStarNZero{} and \HiValPiStarNZero~ppm. Against manual inspection the frontier lies at \PrecPiStarLZero, \MetalPiStarLZero{} and \HiValPiStarLZero~ppm. Holding prevalence at its central value, the edge cell could draw up to \PrecCellPowerStar, \MetalCellPowerStar{} and \HiValCellPowerStar~kW---\PrecCellHeadroom{} to \HiValCellHeadroom{} times the measured value---before the benefit over manual inspection vanishes. For scenarios B and C no break-even exists for grid intensities up to 1.5~kg/kWh, a range that covers all national grids; for the lightweight part of scenario~A the advantage over manual inspection vanishes above \PrecGammaStar~kg/kWh, a level reached only by the most coal-intensive grids. No break-even exists for manual-inspection recall: even perfect manual recall leaves the AI regime ahead, because end-of-line discovery comes too late for rework. Net-negative regimes therefore exist---at very low defect rates, below about \PrecPiStarNZero~ppm for the lightweight part, and for lightweight parts on very carbon-intensive grids.

\subsection{Uncertainty and Global Sensitivity}
Across \MonteCarloDraws{} draws of all \UncertainParams{} uncertain parameters, B3 beats manual inspection in \PrecMcProb\%, \MetalMcProb\% and \HiValMcProb\% of draws, with median $\Delta C$ of \PrecMcMedian, \MetalMcMedian{} and \HiValMcMedian~\kgce{} (5th--95th percentiles in Table~\ref{tab:uncertainty}; Fig.~\ref{fig:uncertainty}, left). The 95th percentile of the edge share of B3's footprint is \PrecMcEdgeShareHigh\%, \MetalMcEdgeShareHigh\% and \HiValMcEdgeShareHigh\%. The PRCC ranking (Fig.~\ref{fig:prcc}) is led by the material carbon factor, defect prevalence, part mass and the detector recall, followed by the collateral escape damage $\kappa$ and the manual-inspection recall; the top coefficients are $\PrecTopPrcc$, $\MetalTopPrcc$ and $\HiValTopPrcc$. All edge-cell parameters---GPU and host power, hardware embodied carbon and lifetime---have $|\mathrm{PRCC}|\le\EdgePrccMax$. Grid intensity acts mainly through rework and review electricity, which B3 increases, so its coefficient is negative; it ranks third in scenario~A, where little embodied carbon is at stake. The material factor ranks first everywhere because its sourced range spans recycled and primary material. Knowing a product's actual material sourcing and escape consequences would narrow the uncertainty far more than better compute measurements.

\subsection{Alert Policy, Workload and the Recall Margin}
B0--B3 share the same edge cell, so differences among them isolate the alert policy. Smoothing alone (B1) removes most false alerts on good parts, but it raises glare alerts, and neither B1 nor persistence without the latch (B2) changes the roughly 150 alerts each defect raises (Table~\ref{tab:policies}); their operator hours differ by at most \BOneBTwoHoursDiffMax\%. The incident latch of B3 collapses repeat alerts to about one per defect. Relative to B0, B3 saves \PrecDeltaHvsBZero, \MetalDeltaHvsBZero{} and \HiValDeltaHvsBZero~operator hours and \PrecDeltaEvsBZero, \MetalDeltaEvsBZero{} and \HiValDeltaEvsBZero~kWh per FU, and $\Delta C=\PrecDeltaCvsBZero$, \MetalDeltaCvsBZero{} and \HiValDeltaCvsBZero~\kgce{}. The Monte Carlo analysis confirms the carbon saving in \PrecMcProbBZero\%, \MetalMcProbBZero\% and \HiValMcProbBZero\% of draws. Two effects limit it. First, the persistence delay costs reworkability where it decays fast: in scenario~C it loses \HiValDelayMaterialCost~kg of material per FU relative to smoothing alone, so B1 emits \HiValBOneCarbonEdge~\kgce{} (under 0.1\%) less than B3 there; B1, however, needs \HiValReviewersBOne{} reviewers where B3 needs one. Second, any recall that persistence loses turns into field escapes. The companion study measured no such loss, but a deployment may differ, so we solve for the recall loss $\delta_r^\star$ at which B3's advantage over B0 vanishes (Fig.~\ref{fig:uncertainty}, right). In scenario~A no such loss exists: B0's review electricity outweighs any escapes recall could avoid. In scenarios B and C the margin is \MetalRecallLossStar{} and \HiValRecallLossStar{} percentage points, so for high-value parts temporal filtering must preserve recall to within a fraction of a point to remain carbon-beneficial.

\caption{Left: Monte Carlo distribution of $\Delta C$ for B3 vs manual inspection (box: quartiles; whiskers: 5th--95th percentile). Right: $\Delta C$ of B3 vs single-frame thresholding B0 as a function of the recall lost to persistence $\delta_r$; markers show the break-even $\delta_r^\star$.}
\label{fig:uncertainty}

\subsection{Carbon-Optimal Detection Thresholds}
Alarm budgets such as ``at most five false alarms per 1{,}000 parts'' are set for operators, not for carbon. For a one-shot station that takes one image per part and diverts it above a threshold, each point of a measured operating curve fixes recall and false-positive rate; the accounting model then gives total carbon, including the review electricity of every false diversion. Fig.~\ref{fig:detector} (right) compares the carbon-optimal threshold with q99 and with the alarm budget over all \OptPairs{} scenario--category pairs. The optimum is never stricter than the budget and is more permissive than q99 in \OptMorePermissive{} pairs, with a median false-positive rate of \OptFprMedian\% against \BudgetFprMedian\% under the budget and up to \OptFprMax\%. Where the detector is weakest the gain is largest: for cable, raising the false-positive rate to \OptFprWorst\% lifts recall from \OptRecallWorstQ{} to \OptRecallWorstOpt{} and saves up to \PrecOptSavingMax, \MetalOptSavingMax{} and \HiValOptSavingMax~\kgce{} per FU in scenarios A, B and C. Constraining the threshold to need no more reviewers than q99 already does leaves the saving almost intact on the slower lines: the capped optimum captures \MetalOptSavingCapShare\% and \HiValOptSavingCapShare\% of the attainable saving in scenarios B and C. On the fast line of scenario~A the unconstrained optimum would need up to \PrecOptRhoMax{} reviewers, and the cap retains \PrecOptSavingCapShare\%. Detection thresholds should therefore be tuned against escape and scrap consequences, with the reviewer budget as a constraint rather than as the objective.

\subsection{Generalisation: A Product Population}
To test whether the conclusions depend on the three reference scenarios, we sample \PopSize{} products: every scenario-specific parameter is drawn log-uniformly over an envelope from half the lowest to twice the highest scenario value, the defect-class mix from a Dirichlet distribution, and all other parameters from their ledger bounds. The full policy beats no inspection for \PopWinNZero\% of the products and manual inspection for \PopWinLZero\%. Fig.~\ref{fig:population} (left) shows that the rule~(\ref{eq:rule}) separates winners from losers exactly: every product lies on the side of the line $\pi=\pi^\star$ that its carbon balance predicts. The edge cell's share of the benefit over manual inspection has a median of \PopEdgeShareMedian\% but exceeds 1\% for \PopEdgeShareAboveOne\% of the products and reaches \PopEdgeShareNinetyFive\% at the 95th percentile (Fig.~\ref{fig:population}, right). Compute becomes relevant only where the quality benefit itself is small: light, low-carbon parts with few defects on slow lines.

Right: cumulative distribution of the edge cell's carbon as a share of the full policy's benefit over manual inspection.}

\subsection{Multi-Criteria Index}
Fig.~\ref{fig:sqi} shows the sub-indicators of B3 against L0. Material and carbon improve, whereas electricity ($S_E=\PrecSE$, $\MetalSE$ and $\HiValSE$) and operator time ($S_H=\PrecSH$, $\MetalSH$ and $\HiValSH$) worsen. The balanced SQI is $\PrecSqiBal$, $\MetalSqiBal$ and $\HiValSqiBal$, and it is positive for \PrecSqiRobust\%, \MetalSqiRobust\% and \HiValSqiRobust\% of all possible weightings. A single index hides a genuine conflict: stakeholders who weight electricity or operator time heavily can rank manual inspection higher even though it emits more carbon. We recommend reporting the sub-indicators and the weight-robustness share, not one score.

\section{Discussion}
\emph{Implications.} For machined and high-value parts the compute footprint of edge inspection is not the decision variable: a laptop-class GPU at line rate sits two to three orders of magnitude below the quality-driven flows. For light, low-carbon parts the margin is thin, and the ``AI is not green'' regime is real: at low defect rates, on carbon-intensive grids, or---across the sampled population---whenever the per-defect benefit $\beta$ is small relative to the cell's per-part carbon $k$. The levers that matter are recall, interception time and alert design. Recall and interception time set escapes and reworkability; alert design decides whether the operator queue is feasible at all, and its workstation electricity can outweigh the scrap savings of a lightweight part. Practitioners should spend their measurement effort on escape consequences, on recall under their own defect distributions and on alert rates, not on inference energy.

\emph{Threats to validity.} (i) Reworkability, rework energy, throughput and manual timing remain scenario assumptions, and prevalence is proxied by scrap rates (Table~\ref{tab:parameters}), and the escape model counts only part replacement, freight and collateral damage, a lower bound that omits customer-side handling. The results are conditional on these choices, and the uncertainty, break-even and population analyses show how the conclusions shift. (ii) The alert rates come from simulated workloads in~\cite{sengar2026paperA}, with synthetic glare and sensor channels; the glare rate is an assumption, and alerts per defect were measured on 2--8~s defect episodes and are applied unchanged regardless of how long a part stays in view. The persistence recall loss is an assumption, which is why we report the recall margin. (iii) We measured only GPU power. Host, camera and lighting enter through $P_{host}$, which leaves the conclusions unchanged even at its upper bound. The GPU also served the host desktop under WSL2, and NVML sensors have documented sampling limitations~\cite{yang2024accurate}; long paced windows, repeats and robust statistics mitigate these effects without removing them. (iv) Detector recall and false-positive rates come from MVTec~AD, a curated laboratory dataset with few nominal test images; production imagery, drift and multi-view stations change them, which the population study and the recall margin bracket. Larger backbones, multi-camera cells or higher frame rates scale $E_{edge}$ proportionally; even a 100-fold increase stays below the frontiers of Fig.~\ref{fig:breakeven}. (v) Reworkability decay, the detect-and-divert architecture, the single-reviewer queue and the replacement-based escape model are simplifications, and rebound effects and end-of-life treatment lie outside the boundary. (vi) We sample parameters independently, ignoring correlations such as that between part mass and material factor.

\section{Conclusion}
With measured inputs---line-rate power of a real PatchCore pipeline, its recall and false-positive rates on \DetCategories{} MVTec~AD categories, and measured alert rates of four alert policies---edge AI inspection is carbon-beneficial in nearly all of the uncertainty space of three reference scenarios, and its edge cell accounts for at most \EdgeOfBenefitMax\% of the benefit it enables over manual inspection. The question reduces to one inequality, $\pi\beta>k$, which held for \PopWinNZero\% of \PopSize{} sampled products against no inspection; compute matters where the per-defect benefit is small---light, low-carbon parts, few defects and carbon-intensive grids. The levers that matter are recall, interception time and alert design: single-frame alerting is operationally infeasible, latched policies save time, electricity and carbon within a quantified recall margin, and detection thresholds tuned for carbon rather than for alarm budgets recover large savings, without extra reviewers on slower lines. All code, raw power traces, detector scores, the parameter ledger and the scripts that generate every figure, table and number in this paper are available at \url{https://github.com/sengarutk/sustainable-edge-quality-intelligence} under the MIT license.
